title: Are taller mountains always wider?
description: The bar graph of the tallest mountains is redrawn with triangles in which the taller triangles are also wider. The table holds only heights, so the widths in the picture say nothing true. Keeko doubts this and says taller mountains are always wider.
teaching_notes: One idea: a picture should show only what the data says, and the data here has heights but no widths. Watch for students who trust a decoration as if it were data.

video_script.why: The child compares the bars of equal width with the triangles of different widths, and sees that the table gives only heights.
video_script.substitution: The tallest mountains of the book are drawn as bars of equal width and as triangles of different widths.
video_script.anchor: the tallest mountain on each continent, drawn once as bars of equal width and once as triangles in which the taller ones are also wider
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko reads the wide triangles as data and says taller mountains are always wider. The table of the book gives only heights and no widths, so the width of a triangle says nothing, and the claim is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: No, the data has only heights, so the wide triangles may mislead us

final_answer.value: No. Width has nothing to do with height; the infographic implies information that may be misleading.
final_answer.spoken: no, the data has only heights, so the wide triangles may mislead us

maths_rules: the table has only heights: 8848, 6962, 6194, 5895, 5642, 4892 and 2228 m
the bar graph draws bars of the same width, so only heights are compared
the triangle picture makes the taller triangles also wider, which adds information the table does not have
the table has no widths, so the width of a triangle says nothing about the mountain
video_script.design: The same seven heights are drawn twice, first as bars of equal width and then as triangles that are wider when taller. The table is then read for what it really holds.
open_questions: The book says the added width may or may not be correct. The worklist answer says width has nothing to do with height. The script says only that the table holds no widths, so the picture adds information the data does not give.
